hpi_details: 74F presents with 2 weeks of progressive mild confusion, difficulty walking (unsteadiness), and a constant dull headache. Daughter recalls her mother fell and bumped her head 3 weeks ago but felt fine initially.

results.value: Left convexity crescentic hypodense subdural collection measuring 1.6 cm with 7 mm rightward midline shift

results.note: Therapeutic anticoagulation remains clinically important in the setting of intracranial bleeding.

clinical_knowledge.topic: Chronic Subdural Hematoma evaluation and management
core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Chronic Subdural Hematoma is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.

Standard management emphasizes Evidence-based diagnostic and therapeutic protocol for Chronic Subdural Hematoma (SDH), likely exacerbated by anticoagulation, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: progressive confusion, balance problems, and headache 3 weeks after a minor fall

Key HPI features: 74F presents with 2 weeks of progressive mild confusion, difficulty walking (unsteadiness), and a constant dull headache. Daughter recalls her mother fell and bumped her head 3 weeks ago but felt fine initially.
Objective/Exam findings: Complete vital signs and focused physical examination required. Diagnostic workup tailored for Chronic Subdural Hematoma (SDH), likely exacerbated by anticoagulation.
Current medications: Amlodipine 5mg daily, Warfarin 2mg daily
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Chronic Subdural Hematoma.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Dementia progression without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.

Ignoring critical warning signs such as: declining consciousness or anticoagulant use, which require urgent CT imaging and reversal of anticoagulation rather than being attributed to progressive dementia.
management_principles: Evidence-based diagnostic and therapeutic protocol for Chronic Subdural Hematoma (SDH), likely exacerbated by anticoagulation
Order urgent non-contrast head CT (look for a crescent-shaped hypodense collection)
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

reference_soap.subjective: A 74-year-old woman presents with progressive confusion, balance problems, and headache after a minor fall 3 weeks ago. She has had 2 weeks of mild confusion, unsteadiness, and a constant dull headache; her daughter reports that she initially felt well after bumping her head.
reference_soap.objective: Complete vital signs and focused physical examination required. Diagnostic workup tailored for Chronic Subdural Hematoma (SDH), likely exacerbated by anticoagulation.
reference_soap.assessment: Clinical presentation highly suggestive of Chronic Subdural Hematoma (SDH), likely exacerbated by anticoagulation.
reference_soap.plan: Evidence-based diagnostic and therapeutic protocol for Chronic Subdural Hematoma (SDH), likely exacerbated by anticoagulation. Order urgent non-contrast head CT (look for crescent-shaped hypodense collection). Check INR and coagulation panel. Refer to neurosurgery for burr hole drainage. Refer to specialty team and provide comprehensive patient counseling.

teaching.one_liner: A slow bleed under the skull after a minor fall weeks earlier, especially in an anticoagulated patient, causing progressive confusion and unsteadiness.
red_flags: Rapidly declining level of consciousness or GCS
Ongoing anticoagulation (warfarin), which increases bleeding risk and may require urgent reversal
Signs of raised intracranial pressure (vomiting, unequal pupils)

must_ask.say: Did your mother fall and hit her head recently?
Is she taking a blood thinner?
How has her confusion and walking changed?
Does she have a constant headache?
How many weeks has this been going on?

history.answer: My mother has been getting increasingly confused, unsteady on her feet, and complaining of a headache over the last couple of weeks.
Before this started, she was completely sharp and independent, cooked her own meals, and had no memory trouble or dementia.
It began about two weeks ago and has been slowly, steadily getting worse each day without fluctuating much.
She has been unusually drowsy, takes several seconds to answer questions, and often mixes up the date and where she is.
No, she has not seen or heard anything unusual, and she does not have any hallucinations or paranoia.
She had a minor fall three weeks ago and bumped her head, but she got right up, felt fine, and never passed out.
Yes, she takes a prescription blood thinner called warfarin every single day for her irregular heartbeat.
She has been wobbling and losing her balance for two weeks, and her right arm seems a little clumsier than usual.
Her face looks fairly symmetric to me and her words are not slurred, though she speaks noticeably slower than normal.
She has had a constant, dull headache for the past two weeks, but she has not had any nausea or vomiting.
No, she has never had convulsions, whole-body twitching, staring spells, or tongue biting.
No, she has not had any urinary or bowel accidents.
No fever or chills at all, and she has had no cough, burning with urination, or foul-smelling urine.
No, her neck is not stiff at all and normal indoor light does not bother her eyes.
She does not have diabetes, she has been eating regular meals, and she does not have excessive thirst or frequent urination.
She is drinking fluids adequately and eating well, with no vomiting, diarrhea, or drop in how much she urinates.
No, she has not started any sleeping pills, painkillers, muscle relaxants, or new prescription drugs lately.
She does not drink any alcohol, and there is no chance she took extra pills by mistake.
She has not mentioned any blurred or double vision.
We do not use indoor gas heaters, and nobody else living in or visiting the home has felt unwell.
She has never had liver cirrhosis or kidney disease, and her skin and eyes are not yellow.
She has never had depression, psychiatric illness, or any episode like this in the past.
I am really scared that she might have had a small stroke, or that she is suddenly developing rapid dementia.
I am deeply worried about the possibility of brain surgery, especially considering her older age and blood thinner.
I really hope she can get a brain CT scan today so we can find out exactly what is causing this.
She has had high blood pressure for ten years and atrial fibrillation for the past five years.
She had an appendectomy when she was a teenager, but no other surgeries or hospitalizations since then.
She takes amlodipine 5 milligrams once daily and warfarin 2 milligrams once daily.
She has no known allergies to any medications or foods.
She has never smoked cigarettes or used tobacco products.
She does not drink alcohol at all.
She is a retired schoolteacher who lives alone in an apartment, but I live down the street and visit her daily.
There is no family history of early dementia, strokes, or bleeding disorders.

exam.finding: Blood pressure 138/82 mmHg, heart rate 76 beats per minute irregularly irregular, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, body temperature 36.7 C, oxygen saturation 98% on ambient air, and capillary fingerstick glucose 108 mg/dL.
Elderly woman appearing mildly lethargic and slow to respond, but sitting comfortably without acute distress or abnormal breath odors.
Glasgow Coma Scale 14 with eye opening 4, verbal response 4, motor response 6; oriented to person but disoriented to exact date and hospital clinic, with mildly reduced attention span.
Faint, non-tender healing contusion on the left frontal scalp without active swelling, laceration, or bony step-off.

Pupils are equal, round, and reactive to light at 3 mm bilaterally; extraocular movements are full without nystagmus; mild flattening of the right nasolabial fold without tongue deviation or bite marks.
Motor strength grade 4+/5 in the right arm and right leg with mild pronator drift, and grade 5/5 throughout the left upper and lower extremities.
Intact and symmetric sensation to light touch across all four extremities.
Deep tendon reflexes 2+ bilaterally, with an equivocal to extensor right plantar reflex and a normal downward flexor left plantar response.
Finger-to-nose coordination is intact bilaterally, but gait is cautious, wide-based, and unsteady, requiring contact guard assistance.
Neck is fully supple with no nuchal rigidity; Kernig and Brudzinski signs are both negative.
Irregularly irregular rhythm with normal first and second heart sounds; no murmurs, rubs, or gallops appreciated.
Abdomen is soft, non-tender, and non-distended, with normal active bowel sounds and no organomegaly or ascites.
